methods.text: Methods
Media, strains and primers

In this study, LB medium (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) and SOC medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) were used for bacterial growth. Competent Escherichia coli DH5α cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific) were employed for transformations.
Primers used in the study (Table 2) were synthesized using a MerMade 4 oligonucleotide synthesizer (LGC Biosearch Technologies, Hoddesdon, UK) at the Genomics Technology Platform of ESSBO.
Table 2: Sets of Primers used in this study
Construct design and synthesis

The inserts for the A and B chains were designed to include an N-terminal His-tag, a start codon (ATG), and a stop codon (TAA). Additionally, overhanging ends compatible with NdeI and XhoI restriction sites were incorporated to facilitate cloning into the predigested pET21a+ plasmid vector. All inserts used in this study are synthesized at the Genomics Technology Platform of ESSBO.
The amino acid sequences of the A and B chains of insulin glargine were retrieved from the DrugBank database (DrugBank ID: DB00047, DrugBank version 5.1.10) (see table 3).

The corresponding nucleotide sequences were derived using the reverse translation tool provided by GenScript. Codon optimization, critical for maximizing expression efficiency in Escherichia coli, was performed using the AI and VectorBuilder codon optimization tool (https://en.vectorbuilder.com/tool/codon-optimization.html). The optimized sequences are presented in Table 3.
Table 3: Peptide and optimized nucleotide sequences

To facilitate cloning, the optimized sequences were further refined by adding linkers to both the 5' and 3' ends, enabling seamless ligation. A start codon (ATG) was introduced at the 5' end to ensure proper initiation of translation. Additionally, a 5' His-tag sequence (MGSSHHHHHHSSGLVPRGS), flanked by flexible linkers, was incorporated to allow efficient protein purification via affinity chromatography. This His-tag includes a thrombin recognition site at its C-terminus, permitting potential cleavage if necessary. A stop codon (TAA) was also added at the 3' end to ensure proper termination of translation. In future constructs, particularly in the A-chain, the thrombin recognition site could be replaced with a TEV protease recognition site to allow complete removal of the His-tag following cleavage.

Complementary strands were generated using the reverse complement tool in the open-source software Benchling (https://benchling.com/). The sequences were then verified against the original peptide sequences using the Expasy translation tool (https://web.expasy.org/translate/). The final optimized sequences selected for synthesis are listed in Table 4.

Benchling was employed to analyze these sequences, confirming the absence of restriction enzyme sites that could interfere with cloning, as well as verifying the absence of repetitive or internal complementary sequences that might lead to secondary structure formation. Cloning simulations within Geneious Prime (version 2024.0.7) were conducted to validate the seamless integration of the target sequences, ensuring they were adequately prepared for synthesis.
Table 4: Final peptide and optimized nucleotide sequences
Optimized sequences synthesis and purification

Single-stranded forward and reverse A and B chain sequences were synthesized using the MerMade 4 oligonucleotide synthesizer (LGC Biosearch Technologies, Hoddesdon, UK), with a Universal Support Column, DMT off (N-iPr), 1000 Å, 1 µmol, MerMade (LGC Biosearch Technologies, Hoddesdon, UK). A specialized protocol optimized for sequences exceeding 130 base pairs was employed (detailed script provided in Table 5).

Purification was performed using an optimized butanol precipitation method. Equal volumes of cold butanol (-20°C) were added to the oligonucleotide solution, followed by 30 seconds of vortexing and a 30-minute incubation at -20°C. The mixture was centrifuged at 14,000 rpm for 15 minutes at 4°C to pellet the oligonucleotides. The pellet was washed twice with 1 mL of 70% ethanol (-20°C), with each wash followed by centrifugation at 14,000 rpm for 10 minutes at 4°C. After air-drying the pellet for 10-15 minutes, the oligonucleotides were resuspended in ultrapure sterile water, resulting in high-purity sequences ready for downstream applications.

The purity and concentration of the synthesized oligonucleotides were verified using a ScanDrop spectrophotometer (Analytik Jena, Germany) and agarose gel electrophoresis (2% agarose gel, Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA; 100V for 45 minutes). This combination ensured accurate assessment of oligonucleotide quality before proceeding to the hybridization step.
Table 5. Optimized DNA synthesis script (1 µmol, 1000 Å, DMT-off, MerMade)
Hybridization of complementary strands

Complementary single-stranded purified sequences were hybridized in a 2x Saline-Sodium Citrate (SSC) buffer containing 0.1% SDS. The buffer was prepared by diluting a 20x SSC stock solution, comprising 3 M NaCl (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), 0.3 M sodium citrate (Biochem Chemopharma, France), and 0.1% SDS (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), adjusted to pH 7.0. For each hybridization reaction, 10 µL of each sequence was mixed with 20 µL of the 2x SSC buffer. The mixture was heated to 95°C for 5 minutes to eliminate potential secondary structures or autohybridization within the synthesized sequences, then gradually cooled to room temperature over 30 minutes to allow proper hybridization. Samples were stored at 4°C for short-term storage and at – 80°C for long-term storage.
Post-hybridization quality assessment and sequence verification

Following hybridization, the integrity and purity of the obtained double-stranded sequences, specifically the A and B chain inserts, were assessed using the ScanDrop and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer, utilizing the DNA 1000 Kit. This kit is designed for analyzing DNA fragments ranging from 25 to 1,000 base pairs, offering a sizing resolution of ±5% and a quantitation reproducibility with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 15% for sequences between 100 and 500 base pairs. Agarose gel electrophoresis (2% agarose gel, Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA; 100V for 45 minutes) was also employed to verify the size and purity of the dsDNA.

Sequencing was performed to confirm the accuracy of the hybridized products and the entirety of the synthesized inserts, using specific primers for the A and B sequences, as detailed in Table 2. The sequencing reactions were conducted using the BigDye™ Terminator v3.1 Cycle Sequencing Kit (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, United States). Each reaction included 20 ng of purified dsDNA in a final volume of 20 µL, comprising 2 µL of BigDye Terminator v3.1, 3 µL of 5× Sequencing buffer, and 1 µL of either forward or reverse primer (3 µM). The PCR cycling conditions were as follows: an initial denaturation at 96°C for 60 seconds, followed by 35 cycles of denaturation at 96°C for 10 seconds, annealing at 50°C for 5 seconds, and extension at 60°C for 4 minutes. The BigDye PCR products were purified using ethanol precipitation.

DNA sequencing was carried out at the Genomics Technology Platform of the Higher School of Biological Sciences of Oran (Oran, Algeria), utilizing an Applied Biosystems 3500 Genetic Analyzer with the POP-7 polymer (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific, United States) for capillary electrophoresis, in accordance with standard sequencing protocols. Alignments of the obtained forward and reverse sequences were performed using Geneious Prime (version 2024.0.7).
Vector preparation and ligation

The expression vector pET21(a)+ was digested with the NdeI and XhoI restriction enzymes to prepare it for the integration of ready-to-ligate double-stranded A-Chain and B inserts, including sticky ends. The reaction mixture consisted of 1 µg of pET21 DNA (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA), 1 µL of NdeI (10 U/µL), 1 µL of XhoI (10 U/µL), and 5 µL of 10× Cutsmart buffer (New England Biolabs, UK), with the final volume adjusted to 50 µL using nuclease-free water. The reaction was incubated at 37°C for 2 hours.

The digested plasmid was run on a 1% agarose gel and subsequently purified using a DNA purification kit suitable for gel extraction (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA). Ligation was performed using a 3:1 molar ratio of insert to vector (calculated using the NEBioCalculator: https://nebiocalculator.neb.com/#!/ligation). The ligation reaction included 50 ng of digested pET21 vector, an appropriate amount of the insert, 1 µL of T4 DNA ligase (400 U/µL, Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA) and 2 µL of 10× T4 DNA ligase buffer (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA, USA), with a total reaction volume of 20 µL. The ligation was incubated at 16°C for 2 hours, followed by an overnight incubation at 4°C.
Post-ligation verification and transformation

The ligated products were first analyzed using ScanDrop and a Bioanalyzer to confirm the integrity and size of the constructs. This was followed by agarose gel electrophoresis (2% agarose gel, Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA; 100V for 45 minutes) to assess purity. Competent E. coli DH5α cells (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) were transformed with the ligated plasmids using a standard transformation protocol, which included a 50-second heat shock at 42°C, followed by recovery in SOC medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The transformed cells were then plated on LB agar containing 100 µg/mL ampicillin (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA). Colonies were screened by colony PCR using T7 and insert-specific primers to verify the presence of the insert. Positive clones were further subjected to plasmid extraction using a plasmid miniprep kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA). The presence of the inserts was subsequently confirmed by sequencing, and in silico analysis was performed using Geneious Prime (version 2024.0.7).
